Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
There's a big two-page advert for Sabbat war in Scrye. A couple of
points:

* Lucita gets a of lot attention with the byline "Lucita of Clan
Lasombra. Shadows kill at her command."

* There's a slogan "Make and break alliances as you eliminate your
foes."

It's this latter point which concerns me as the game seems a bit
schizo here. There was a fair amount of table talk and cross-table
action in our games last night. This seems quite feasible but seems
to cause more bad feelings than in other games like Shadowfist.
Partly it's because of the presumption that players ought to be
attacking their prey instead and partly because one is constantly in
fear for one's position as the blood pool dries up and Final Death
approaches.

I know that Garfield tried to design the game to eliminate
multi-player diplomacy but don't think that he succeeded. It's
interesting to see this feature of the game being promoted now.

Andrew

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
>
> There's a big two-page advert for Sabbat war in Scrye. A couple of
> points:
>
> * Lucita gets a of lot attention with the byline "Lucita of Clan
> Lasombra. Shadows kill at her command."
>
> * There's a slogan "Make and break alliances as you eliminate your
> foes."
>
> It's this latter point which concerns me as the game seems a bit
> schizo here. There was a fair amount of table talk and cross-table
> action in our games last night. This seems quite feasible but seems
> to cause more bad feelings than in other games like Shadowfist.
> Partly it's because of the presumption that players ought to be
> attacking their prey instead and partly because one is constantly in
> fear for one's position as the blood pool dries up and Final Death
> approaches.

Players "ought to be" maximizing their VPs - in whatever manner
they can. Making deals to go across table in return for some boost to
one's position or ability to harvest another VP (as one perceives it) is
common. Attacking one's prey is the obvious way to increase VPs, of course.

> I know that Garfield tried to design the game to eliminate
> multi-player diplomacy but don't think that he succeeded. It's
> interesting to see this feature of the game being promoted now.

Garfield did not design the game to eliminate multi-player diplomacy
(the voting rules are proof of that). That feature has always been
a big selling point of the game. Garfield *did* attempt to eliminate
the "king-maker"(*) aspect inherent to so many multi-player games (as
he stated in an interview in an old issue of Scrye), which many
players find distasteful (at least from what I can tell from reading
rec.games.board). Garfield attempted to decrease the king-maker aspect
by, e.g., allowing bleed to be directed only at the prey by default (and
the two bleed actions that one could direct elsewhere in the base set
were both capped to bleed for no more than one). A player might still
be able to play "king-maker" with her decisions to attack or to defend,
or with votes or rush combat, but these are harder to restrict, and
harder to implement effectively from a losing position anyhow.

(*) "King-maker" refers to the ability of a player with a "lost"
position (one who no longer has any chance of winning) to force
any of the other remaining players to win (or lose) through his
actions, almost without regard to those other players' positions and
resources.

--

Messages.Author: Noal McDonald
Messages.Body:
a...@csi.com wrote:
> There was a fair amount of table talk and cross-table
> action in our games last night.

As well it should. VTES, unlike other CCGs, encourages a social aspect
to it's strategy, much like poker. I've always felt that the best
players of VTES were not the people that put together the best decks,
but the people that played the table to their best advantage. A mediocre
deck in the hands of a skilled player is usually more effective than a
great deck in the hands of a mediocre player. That's why some people
seem do well in tournaments no matter what type of deck they play and
some people never seem to make the finals.

> This seems quite feasible but seems to cause more bad feelings
> than in other games like Shadowfist. Partly it's because of the
> presumption that players ought to be attacking their prey instead
> and partly because one is constantly in fear for one's position
> as the blood pool dries up and Final Death approaches.

It's a fool that ignores the rest of the table. Just because a player
isn't a predator or prey, that doesn't make them your new best friend.
Very often it is to your best advantage to attack cross table to keep a
player from steam rolling the table.

> I know that Garfield tried to design the game to eliminate
> multi-player diplomacy

You "know" wrong. This is starting to be a theme, Andrew. If I hadn't
met you in person, I would have thought you a teenager with all the
things that you "know". You would do well to gain more experience in the
game before making assumptions about it.

Regards,
Noal

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 04 Aug 2000 08:14:28 -0400, LSJ wrote:

>Players "ought to be" maximizing their VPs - in whatever manner
>they can.

This works well in tournaments I expect. It's not so easy to retain
this focus in a one-off, social game where there are other
considerations like

* being the winner (coming second is coming nowhere)
* having fun (through role-playing, vengeance &c)
* getting a lost game over with quickly

I suggested that we keep a running total of VP to help our group
retain the correct focus but, without a formal system to copy, I doubt
that anything will come of it.

>Garfield did not design the game to eliminate multi-player diplomacy
>(the voting rules are proof of that). That feature has always been
>a big selling point of the game. Garfield *did* attempt to eliminate
>the "king-maker"(*) aspect inherent to so many multi-player games (as
>he stated in an interview in an old issue of Scrye), which many
>players find distasteful

I don't agree. As I see it, the key mechanic that distinguishes
Vampire from most other multi-player CCG is the attack-to-the-left
system. This is designed to stop players forming coalitions to oust
other players in a free-for-all way. As I understand it, he wanted to
stop the game from being dominated by traditional multi-player
diplomacy - something which he feels has been done to death elsewhere.

One price of this is that it encourages king-making, in my view. Your
predator is quite implacable because, apart from those rare effects
which change the seating order, you both know that he's coming to get
you. If your predator establishes dominance over you to the point
that your position is doomed then you have little else to do but play
king-maker - there's nothing you can say to him that would persuade
him to attack someone else.

Anyway, this is somewhat beside the point. To be clear, this was my
surprise that the game is being promoted as a traditional type of
wheeler-dealer, multi-player game when, to my mind, Vampire's unique
selling proposition is that it is less dominated by this aspect than
most.

Andrew

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <DFF66245950804C7.61C0E339...@lp.airnew

s.net>, Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> writes

>I suggested that we keep a running total of VP to help our group
>retain the correct focus but, without a formal system to copy, I doubt
>that anything will come of it.

Erm, do you really need a formal system to tot up VPs?

Here's one if you do:

- At the end of a game, write down how many VPs each player got on a
sheet of paper. Use the same sheet of paper for all games, until it
gets full. Repeat with another piece of paper as necessary

- When a player asks how many points they have got in total, total the
number of points they have on the sheet(s)

--

James Coupe

>>they can.
>

>I suggested that we keep a running total of VP to help our group
>retain the correct focus but, without a formal system to copy, I doubt
>that anything will come of it.

It occurs to me that using the Ante rule is a good way of maintaining
the correct focus in social games with no need for record-keeping. No
doubt the rule has been discarded in most groups, as happened with
Magic but it's a shame to waste the cards which relate to this. And
it's a good way of restraining the player with lots of power rares
without recourse to a card limit or moral pressure.

We haven't tried this rule yet and we'd have to figure out a way of
handling players using borrowed decks. Is anyone else out there
playing this way?

Andrew

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 08 Aug 2000 13:07:19 +0100, Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com>
wrote:

>It occurs to me that using the Ante rule is a good way of maintaining
>the correct focus in social games with no need for record-keeping. No

I suggest that playing for ante with your friends is an excellent way
to turn the games cut-throat, anti-social, much more serious, and
much, much, much less than fun. Since you know which card you're
anteing, when it turns out to be your solitary Protected Resources
that it took you FOREVER and a day to get, you're going to be VERY
pissy from the word 'go', and even more pissy if you lose it. I know
I would be much less than happy. It will be the same for everyone,
except for the guy who's anteing Lucky Blow. He won't give a damn.

Why would you use Protected Resources in a social game? Perhaps
you're testing out an idea. Who knows? It's your deck, it's your
business. But PR just happens to be THE most rare card in the game.
Losing it to cheesy ante and putting a hole in your collection would
be just stupid.

>doubt the rule has been discarded in most groups, as happened with
>Magic but it's a shame to waste the cards which relate to this. And

No it's not. This is Jyhad, not marbles. And look closely at some of
those cards - High Stakes? "Ante another card or be ousted." A
Ventrue deck could really put a beating on your cards with this, not
like the Ventrue aren't already inherently a strong clan or anything.

>it's a good way of restraining the player with lots of power rares
>without recourse to a card limit or moral pressure.

First: Why should the player with lots of rare cards need to be
restrained? It's possible to build decks out of all common and
uncommon cards that will defeat "rare" decks. If someone wants to
play with a bunch of wack rares, LET THEM.

Second: the concept of "power rare" doesn't really exist in V:TES.
Even Awe, a hideously good and rare card, has its inherent drawback of
needing a Voter Cap along with it to avoid emptying the blood off your
vamp. Sometimes it's better to just use the Bewitching Oration - a
blisteringly common card.

Third: It's not a "good" way of restraint in any case. Under the
ante rules, I would never play a deck that had anything but commons +
uncommons in it - too much effort getting the rares in the first place
to let luck take them away. Actually, I'd probably quit playing with
that group completely, because it wouldn't be any fun for me anymore.
This may restrain me and make the rest of the group happy, but it
equates to social and/or moral pressure on the group's part, and loses
a player, which is pretty much a bad thing.

>We haven't tried this rule yet and we'd have to figure out a way of
>handling players using borrowed decks. Is anyone else out there
>playing this way?

Not that we know of. Most people had a look at the ante rules,
retched loudly, and continued on. I've played in a couple of draft
tournaments where the ante rules and cards were used, but that's
different - since it's a draft tournament, they're not really "my"
cards anyway until the end of the tournament. And since I put forth
no effort to go out and get them in the first place, I don't really
mind watching them get ante'd away.

If I had drafted a card I really couldn't possibly stand the thought
of giving up, then I would probably have just not put it in my draft
deck and kept it aside. But more likely than not, I'd have stuck it
in my deck and tried to win with it. Again, though, this is draft.

-- Derek
Jack-Booted Thug of Atlanta

Messages.Author: inr...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
>
> We haven't tried this rule yet and we'd have to figure out a way of
> handling players using borrowed decks. Is anyone else out there
> playing this way?
>

> Andrew

The Group here in Madison does. It works out alright so far, although,
in this case we play a limited set (9 boosters each) so that someone
doesn't end up losing cards in their constructed decks. It's played
seperatly. We still keep track of VP's, and when you oust someone you
can take either their ante card or something from their sideboard.
Also, a player antes the top two cards after a cut, and then protects
one, shuffleing it back into the deck. Although, with the limited card
set, the decks aren't tournement winners, they are compedative amongst
themselves.

On a personal note, i think you get a better card mix with a starter
and two boosters (IMHO) but mixing them is bad. The extra commons make
the starter based decks usually more lethal than the just boosters.

This makes for an interesting game play, but to cover another base,
ante in a constucted arena is kind of a non-starter. Mainly because
with everyone able to choose from a larger card set you can't quite use
them to keep track of wins. Even in our restricted environment, we
still write down VP wins.

If you're more interested in this concept i suggest contacting Adrian,
aka the corruptor about it.

Cameron

PS, looking forward to meeting everyone at gencon
